title: Nuclear fission and fusion
examTip: Fission and fusion both release energy through a change in total nuclear mass. But they work in opposite directions. Fission: a large nucleus splits into two smaller ones. Fusion: two small nuclei join into a larger one. Know which fuels each one uses: U-235 or Pu-239 for fission, and hydrogen isotopes for fusion.
introTips: Each nuclear reaction releases millions of times more energy than a chemical reaction like burning. That is why a tiny amount of fuel gives so much power.
Fission is what happens inside every nuclear power station today. It is proven technology.
Fusion powers the Sun and all stars. But we can't yet keep it going long enough, or cheaply enough, to make electricity commercially.
In a chain reaction, each fission releases neutrons that can trigger more fissions. Without control, this becomes an explosion (atomic bomb). Under control, it powers a reactor.
Nuclear power makes no carbon dioxide while it runs. But radioactive waste must be stored safely for thousands of years.
intro: When Einstein wrote E = mc², he pointed to something amazing. Mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, and you can convert between them. Nuclear reactions do exactly this. A tiny loss of mass releases an enormous amount of energy. Fission powers nuclear submarines, aircraft carriers and about 10% of the world's electricity. Fusion powers every star in the universe. Its energy has made life on Earth possible. Scientists have been trying to harness fusion since the 1950s. If they succeed, it could give almost limitless clean energy. It is one of the biggest engineering challenges in history.

keyPoints.heading: Nuclear fission
keyPoints.content: In nuclear fission, a large unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron. It then splits into two smaller nuclei, called fission fragments. It also releases 2 or 3 neutrons and a large amount of energy. The energy comes out as kinetic energy of the fragments and as gamma radiation. The most common fuels are uranium-235 (U-235) and plutonium-239 (Pu-239). These nuclei are large enough to become unstable after absorbing a neutron, so they split. Each fission reaction releases about 200 MeV. A chemical reaction releases only a few eV. That is about 50 million times less. This is why such small amounts of nuclear fuel give so much energy. The two smaller nuclei produced (fission fragments) are radioactive themselves. They must be managed as nuclear waste.
writeBullets: Fission: large nucleus absorbs a neutron → splits into two smaller nuclei + 2–3 neutrons + energy
Fuels: uranium-235 (U-235) or plutonium-239 (Pu-239)
Releases ~200 MeV per reaction. That is millions of times more energy than a chemical reaction
Fission fragments are radioactive. They must be stored as nuclear waste
Energy is released as kinetic energy of the fragments and as gamma radiation

keyTerms.def: A large nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing 2–3 neutrons and a large amount of energy
One of the two smaller nuclei produced when a large nucleus undergoes fission; typically radioactive
A fissile isotope used as fuel in nuclear reactors; splits when it absorbs a slow neutron

keyPoints.memTip: Fission = split. Large nucleus + neutron → two smaller nuclei + 2–3 neutrons + enormous energy.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to describe the process step by step. Use this order. Neutron absorbed → nucleus splits → new nuclei + more neutrons + energy.

keyPoints.heading: Chain reactions and controlling fission
keyPoints.content: Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons. These neutrons can go on to trigger more fissions, which each release more neutrons. This is a chain reaction. Uncontrolled chain reaction: each fission triggers several more. The number grows exponentially → an explosive release of energy → a nuclear weapon (atomic bomb). Controlled chain reaction: the rate is kept steady. One neutron from each fission goes on to trigger exactly one more fission. This is done using: - Control rods: these absorb extra neutrons. Push them in to slow the reaction down. Pull them out to speed it up. They are made of boron or cadmium. - Moderator: this slows neutrons down to the right speed for U-235 to absorb them. It is usually water or graphite. In a nuclear power station, the heat from fission makes steam. The steam drives turbines and generates electricity. This is just like a traditional power station, but it uses nuclear fuel instead of burning fossil fuels.
writeBullets: Chain reaction: neutrons from each fission trigger more fissions → a process that keeps itself going
Uncontrolled: exponential growth → explosion (nuclear weapon)
Controlled: each fission triggers exactly one more → a steady energy release in a reactor
Control rods: absorb neutrons. Pushing them in slows the reaction; pulling them out speeds it up (boron or cadmium)
Moderator: slows neutrons to a speed U-235 can absorb (usually water or graphite)

keyTerms.def: Each fission event releases neutrons that trigger further fissions — self-sustaining if controlled, explosive if uncontrolled
Rods of boron or cadmium inserted into a reactor to absorb neutrons and control the rate of fission
Material (water or graphite) that slows neutrons to the correct speed for absorption by U-235

keyPoints.memTip: Control rods in → fewer neutrons → reaction slows. Control rods out → more neutrons → reaction speeds up.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to draw or describe the chain reaction diagram: one fission → 2–3 neutrons → more fissions. Show why it multiplies.

keyPoints.heading: Nuclear fusion
keyPoints.content: In nuclear fusion, two small nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus. This releases large amounts of energy. The most studied reaction for making energy uses deuterium (²H) and tritium (³H). These are two isotopes of hydrogen. They combine to form helium plus a neutron plus energy: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + energy. Fusion releases even more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission. Fusion is the energy source of stars, including the Sun. In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium. This happens under enormous gravitational pressure, at temperatures of ~15 million °C. Advantages over fission: more energy per kg, plenty of fuel (hydrogen), and no long-lived radioactive waste. Challenge: it needs extremely high temperatures (~100 million °C on Earth) and pressures. These overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei. Keeping these conditions long enough to make net energy has not yet been done at commercial scale.
writeBullets: Fusion: two small nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus + energy
Typical reaction: deuterium + tritium → helium + neutron + energy
Powers all stars, including the Sun. It happens at millions of °C and extreme pressure
Releases more energy per kg than fission. The fuel is plentiful. No long-lived waste
Not yet commercially viable. On Earth it needs ~100 million °C to overcome electrostatic repulsion

keyTerms.def: Two small nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus, releasing energy — the process that powers stars
Hydrogen isotopes used as fuel in fusion reactions; abundant and available from seawater (deuterium)
The force between two positively charged nuclei that must be overcome for fusion to occur — requires very high temperatures

keyPoints.memTip: Fusion = join. Small + small → bigger + energy.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be clear on WHY fusion needs such high temperatures. It gives nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome the electrostatic repulsion. Then they can get close enough to fuse.

keyPoints.heading: Comparing fission and fusion — nuclear power evaluation
keyPoints.content: Fission advantages: proven technology and large-scale electricity generation. It makes no CO₂ while running. It is reliable, because it does not depend on the weather. Fission disadvantages: - radioactive waste stays hazardous for thousands of years and needs secure storage - risk of accidents (Chernobyl, Fukushima) - high building cost - uranium fuel will run out one day, so it is not truly renewable - risk of nuclear weapons spreading, as the waste can be used for weapons Fusion advantages: more energy per kg, and almost limitless fuel (hydrogen from seawater). No long-lived radioactive waste, no CO₂ and no meltdown risk. Fusion disadvantages: it needs conditions not yet possible at commercial scale (100 million °C). It is a huge engineering challenge. It has needed enormous investment for decades, with no commercial output yet. People joke that it is 'always 30 years away'. Both processes release energy because of a small change in nuclear mass. This mass difference is converted to energy by E = mc².
writeBullets: Fission: no CO₂, reliable, proven. But long-lived radioactive waste, accident risk, limited fuel
Fusion: limitless fuel, no long-lived waste, more energy per kg. But not yet commercially viable
Both: no CO₂ emissions while running. Energy comes from a mass change (E = mc²)
Fusion challenge: 100 million °C needed to overcome electrostatic repulsion between nuclei
Nuclear waste from fission must be stored safely for thousands of years. A major political and engineering challenge

keyTerms.def: Radioactive fission fragments and other materials from nuclear reactors — remain hazardous for thousands of years
Einstein's equation showing the relationship between mass and energy — a tiny loss of mass produces enormous energy in nuclear reactions

keyPoints.memTip: Fission = proven, but has a waste problem. Fusion = ideal, but not yet working commercially.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Evaluation questions about nuclear power are common 6-mark questions. Practise writing a balanced argument with the advantages and disadvantages of fission. Then compare it with fusion.

0.question: In nuclear fission, what triggers a uranium-235 nucleus to split?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! The U-235 nucleus absorbs a slow neutron. This makes it unstable enough to split into two smaller nuclei. It also releases 2–3 more neutrons.
0.wrongFeedback: Fission starts when a U-235 nucleus absorbs a slow neutron. This makes it unstable, so it splits. It releases more neutrons and a large amount of energy.

1.question: What is the role of control rods in a nuclear reactor?
options: They absorb neutrons to control the rate of fission
They slow neutrons down to the speed U-235 needs to absorb them
They cool the reactor by absorbing heat from the fuel
They shield the reactor from radiation
1.correctFeedback: Correct! Control rods (made of boron or cadmium) absorb neutrons. Push them further in → fewer neutrons → the reaction slows. Pull them out → more neutrons → the reaction speeds up.
1.wrongFeedback: Control rods absorb neutrons. This is how they control the reaction rate. The moderator (water or graphite) is what slows the neutrons down. These are two different parts with different jobs.

2.question: Why is nuclear fusion not used yet to generate electricity on a large scale?
options: It needs temperatures of around 100 million °C, which are very hard to keep going. It has not yet made net energy at commercial scale
The fuel (uranium) needed for fusion is very rare and costly
Fusion produces more radioactive waste than fission
Fusion reactions are too small to make useful amounts of energy
2.correctFeedback: Correct! On Earth, fusion needs extreme temperatures (~100 million °C). These overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positive nuclei. Keeping this going long enough to make net energy has not yet been done commercially.
2.wrongFeedback: Fusion uses hydrogen isotopes as fuel, not uranium. They are plentiful. The problem is the extreme conditions needed: ~100 million °C to overcome electrostatic repulsion. This has not yet been kept going long enough for commercial energy.

3.question: Which of these is a disadvantage of making electricity by nuclear fission?
options: It makes radioactive waste that stays dangerous for thousands of years
It gives out a lot of carbon dioxide while it runs
It only works when the weather is right
Its fuel will never run out
3.correctFeedback: Correct! Fission waste stays radioactive for thousands of years. It has to be stored safely.
3.wrongFeedback: Fission makes no carbon dioxide while it runs and does not depend on the weather. Its uranium fuel will run out one day. Its big problem is long-lived radioactive waste.

commonMistakes: Mixing up fission and fusion. Fission splits a large nucleus. Fusion joins two small ones. A useful memory: Fission = Fragment (split apart); Fusion = Fuse (join together).
Saying the moderator controls the reaction rate. The moderator slows neutrons to the right speed. The control rods control the reaction rate by absorbing neutrons.
Thinking fusion makes lots of radioactive waste, like fission. Fusion's main product is helium. Its radioactivity is much shorter-lived than that of fission fragments.
Forgetting that fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons (not just 1). This is what makes the chain reaction possible.
Saying that nuclear power produces CO₂. It does not while running. Building the plant and processing the fuel do cause CO₂, but generating the electricity does not.
examTips: For chain reaction questions, explain the process step by step. Neutron absorbed by U-235 → splits → releases 2–3 neutrons → these trigger more fissions → chain reaction.
Control rods vs moderator: control rods absorb neutrons (controlling the rate). The moderator slows neutrons (so they can be absorbed). Know both, and don't mix them up.
In evaluation questions about nuclear power, give both advantages and disadvantages. A one-sided answer will not get full marks on a 6-marker.
For fusion questions, always explain WHY a high temperature is needed. It gives nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome the repulsion between positive charges. Then they get close enough to fuse.
revisionCardBullets: Fission: large nucleus + neutron → 2 smaller nuclei + 2–3 neutrons + energy
Chain reaction: each fission triggers more. Controlled (reactor) or uncontrolled (bomb)
Control rods: absorb neutrons and control the reaction rate (boron or cadmium)
Moderator: slows neutrons for absorption by U-235 (water or graphite)
Fusion: two small nuclei (for example, deuterium + tritium) combine → a larger nucleus + energy
Fusion powers the Sun and all stars
Fusion needs ~100 million °C to overcome electrostatic repulsion
Fusion: more energy per kg, plenty of fuel, no long-lived waste. But not yet commercially viable
Fission: no CO₂ while running. But long-lived radioactive waste is a major challenge
Both fission and fusion: energy comes from a tiny change in nuclear mass (E = mc²)
